# SoulGuard

> A Python library for tamper-evident agent memory (a SHA-256 hash chain), per-agent Ed25519 and hybrid Ed25519 + ML-DSA-44 signing keys ("SoulKeys"), HMAC capability tokens, and an OWASP ASI06 tamper scan. Apache-2.0, by Saluca LLC.

Facts agents most often get wrong: the core (memory, governance, detection) is standard library only, Python 3.9+; identity needs `cryptography`, hybrid keys also need `quantcrypt`. It is installed from this GitHub repository only, never from PyPI (a PyPI project with the same name is not this one). It detects edits to stored entries, splices, reorders and stripped or forged signatures; it does not detect deletion of entries from the end of a chain, false content written through `append()`, or tool calls that skip `verify_token()`.

Generated 2026-10-22 from the files below. Regenerate whenever any of them changes.

## README.md

# SoulGuard

**An open trust layer for AI-agent memory and identity.** Tamper-evident memory, per-agent cryptographic identity, capability-scoped governance tokens, and OWASP-**ASI06** memory-poisoning detection, so that after-the-fact edits to a stateful agent's stored history are detected rather than silent.

Apache-2.0 · by [Saluca LLC](https://saluca.com) · extracted from the production stack that runs **Alfred**, a sovereign agentic operating partner.

> **Correction, 2026-10-22.** An accuracy check of this README against the code on `main` found three
> claims that said more than the code does. What the README said, and what is true:
>
> 1. *"Any later edit breaks the chain and is detected."* An in-place edit of a stored entry is
>    detected, and so is a spliced or reordered entry. Two edits are not: **deleting entries from the
>    end of the chain** passes `verify()` and `scan()`, signed or not, because nothing in the chain
>    records its own length; and a chain **rebuilt consistently** by someone with write access passes
>    unless its entries are signed and checked against a public key you pinned out of band. To catch
>    truncation, keep the head hash (`mem.head`) somewhere the writer cannot reach and compare it.
> 2. *"SoulKeys ... catch impersonation & persona drift."* SoulKeys catch forged or stripped
>    signatures. There is no persona-drift detection in the code.
> 3. *"Even a partially-compromised agent can't exceed its authority."* `governance` mints and checks
>    HMAC capability tokens. It does not intercept tool calls: authority is enforced only where your
>    code calls `verify_token()` before acting, and anyone holding the shared secret can mint any scope.
>
> The table below is corrected. The rest of the text is unchanged except for punctuation.

---

## Why

AI agents became *stateful*: they carry persistent **memory**, a durable **identity**, and tool access. That state is also the new attack surface. In 2026 OWASP named **Memory Poisoning (ASI06)** a top-10 agentic risk: once memory is the substrate, an injected lie persists across sessions and the agent later acts on it with full authority, the machine equivalent of confabulation. Input-only guardrails don't see the corrupted state that already lives inside the agent.

SoulGuard makes agent memory and identity **first-class, verifiable, owned primitives**:

| Module | What it does |
|---|---|
| `memory` | **Hash-chained, tamper-evident memory.** An in-place edit, a splice or a reorder breaks the chain and is *detected*, not silent. Tail truncation is not detected without a head hash held out of band (see the correction above). |
| `identity` | **Per-agent cryptographic identity (SoulKeys, Ed25519, or quantum-ready hybrid Ed25519 + ML-DSA-44).** Sign memories and messages; a forged or stripped signature is caught when you verify with the agent's public key. |
| `governance` | **Capability-scoped, short-lived, least-privilege tokens** (HMAC-SHA256, default TTL 300 s). Your code checks a token before each action; an action outside the token's scopes or after expiry is refused at that check. |
| `detection` | **ASI06 scan.** Turns silent tampering into a classified alarm: `content_tampered`, `broken_link` (injection or reorder), `bad_signature`, `missing_signature`. |

## Status

Experimental, v0.1.0. What works today, all of it covered by the 25 tests in `tests/`:

- hash-chained memory with tamper, splice, reorder and signature-stripping detection;
- Ed25519 SoulKeys and hybrid Ed25519 + ML-DSA-44 SoulKeys (both-or-reject);
- HMAC capability tokens with scope and expiry checks;
- `scan()`, which reports whether signatures were actually checked (`signatures_verified`);
- a v0 ASI06 benchmark harness with a fixed seed.

What it does not do: detect a false memory written through the normal `append()` path (SoulGuard is the integrity layer, not a content filter), detect deletion of entries from the end of a chain, or enforce tokens on your behalf. The ASI06 harness injects only two attack types (an in-place content edit and an out-of-band entry), both of which the hash chain catches by construction, so its 1.000 detection rate is a regression check, not evidence against an adaptive adversary.

Planned and not yet built: hardening, a formal third-party security audit, expanded reference implementations, MCP adapters, and a published adversarial benchmark (see [`docs/THREAT_MODEL.md`](docs/THREAT_MODEL.md)).

## Install

Tested 2026-10-22 on Python 3.12.10 (CI runs 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13; `pyproject.toml` declares 3.9+).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/saluca-labs/soulguard
cd soulguard
# core (memory + governance + detection) is pure standard library: nothing to install
python examples/quickstart.py        # watch a poisoning attack get caught
python tests/test_soulguard.py       # run the core tests
python benchmark/asi06_harness.py    # ASI06 detection benchmark v0

# identity (SoulKeys) needs cryptography:
pip install cryptography
# quantum-ready hybrid SoulKeys (Ed25519 + ML-DSA-44) also need quantcrypt.
# Install SoulGuard itself from this repository, pinned to a commit or tag:
pip install "soulguard[pqc] @ git+https://github.com/saluca-labs/soulguard@283d0192b29374859221e3d469182ff29c1ac16d"

# development: all extras plus pytest, then the full suite
pip install -e ".[dev]"
python -m pytest
```

SoulGuard is distributed as source from this GitHub repository only. It is not
published on PyPI, and a PyPI package named `soulguard` is not ours: never
install it from PyPI. Pin the git install to a tag or commit you
have reviewed (the commit above is an example; replace it with the ref you want).

## Quickstart

```bash
python examples/quickstart.py
```

Output from a clean clone on 2026-10-22:

```
=== SoulGuard quickstart ===

1) Clean history:
   OK -3 memory entries verified, no poisoning detected; signatures NOT verified (no verifier supplied).

2) Attacker silently rewrites memory #1 (the IOC sighting)...
   ALERT -poisoning detected in 1 of 3 entries (first at #1): content_tampered at [1]
   intact=False  first_compromised_index=1

3) Capability-scoped governance:
   token grants memory:read -> True
   token grants tool:exec   -> False (correctly denied)

Done. Poisoning detected, authority scoped. That's the trust layer.
```

## Usage

### 30-second example

```python
from soulguard import TamperEvidentMemory, scan

mem = TamperEvidentMemory(agent_id="alfred")
mem.append("IOC 8.8.8.8 observed on 2026-06-20.")
mem.append("Playbook RB-17 applied; ticket closed.")

scan(mem).intact            # True, clean history

mem.entries[0].content = "No IOCs were ever observed."   # ASI06 poisoning
print(scan(mem).summary())  # ALERT -poisoning detected in 1 of 2 entries (first at #0): content_tampered at [0]
```

Add cryptographic attribution:

```python
from soulguard import SoulKey, TamperEvidentMemory, scan
key = SoulKey()
mem = TamperEvidentMemory(agent_id=key.agent_id)
mem.append("signed memory", signer=key)
scan(mem, verifier=key.public()).intact   # True; a forged sig would flag bad_signature
```

Quantum-ready: same API, hybrid keys (a break of Ed25519 *or* ML-DSA-44 alone can't forge):

```python
from soulguard import HybridSoulKey, TamperEvidentMemory, scan
key = HybridSoulKey()                       # Ed25519 + ML-DSA-44, both-or-reject
mem = TamperEvidentMemory(agent_id=key.agent_id)
mem.append("post-quantum signed memory", signer=key)
scan(mem, verifier=key.public()).intact     # True
```

All three snippets were run on 2026-10-22 and print what the comments say.

### Capability tokens

```python
from soulguard import issue_token, verify_token
secret = b"per-deployment-signing-secret"
tok = issue_token(secret, agent_id="alfred", scopes=["memory:read"], ttl_seconds=300)
verify_token(secret, tok, "memory:read")   # True
verify_token(secret, tok, "tool:exec")     # False
```

### Chains that began before signing

`verify(verifier=..., signed_from_idx=N)` and `scan(..., signed_from_idx=N)` excuse a missing
signature below entry `N` (it is counted in `ScanResult.unsigned_prefix`), never an invalid one.
Supply `N` from your own configuration, never from a field stored in the chain.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[agent] -->|append content, signer| M[memory.TamperEvidentMemory]
  M -->|entries| D[detection.scan]
  K[identity.SoulKey / HybridSoulKey] -->|sign entry hash| M
  K -->|public key, pinned| D
  D --> R[ScanResult: intact, findings, signatures_verified]
  G[governance.issue_token] --> T[capability token]
  T --> V[governance.verify_token, called by your code before each action]
```

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `src/soulguard/memory.py` | `TamperEvidentMemory`, `MemoryEntry`, `Finding`; SHA-256 over canonical JSON, each entry linked to the previous hash |
| `src/soulguard/identity.py` | `SoulKey` / `SoulKeyVerifier` (Ed25519) and `HybridSoulKey` / `HybridSoulKeyVerifier` (Ed25519 + ML-DSA-44) |
| `src/soulguard/governance.py` | `issue_token`, `verify_token` (HMAC-SHA256, scopes, expiry) |
| `src/soulguard/detection.py` | `scan`, `ScanResult` |
| `benchmark/asi06_harness.py` | ASI06 benchmark v0 |
| `docs/THREAT_MODEL.md` | assets, adversary, attack classes, residual risk |

The core imports only the standard library; `identity` is imported only if `cryptography` (and, for
the hybrid keys, `quantcrypt`) is installed.

## Design principles

- **Local-first / sovereign:** runs where *you* control it; no platform owns your agent's memory.
- **Verifiable, not trusted:** integrity is checkable, not asserted.
- **Dependency-light core:** the memory/governance/detection core is standard-library only.

## docs/THREAT_MODEL.md

# SoulGuard Threat Model: Agent Memory Poisoning (OWASP ASI06)

*v0, 2026-06-24. Scope: the integrity and attributability of a stateful AI agent's persistent memory and identity. Maps to OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications **ASI06, Memory & Context Poisoning**.*

> **Correction, 2026-10-22.** Two statements in this document said more than the code does.
> (1) The benchmark paragraph below said the harness reports a **first-detection index**; it reports
> detection rate, false-positive rate and the number missed, not a first-detection index (that value
> is available per scan as `ScanResult.first_compromised_index`). (2) The residual-risk list omitted
> **tail truncation**: deleting entries from the end of a chain passes `verify()` and `scan()`, signed
> or not, because the chain does not record its own length. Detecting it needs the head hash held
> outside the writer's reach. Both are added below; nothing else in the analysis changes.

## Assets to protect
1. **Agent memory:** the persistent record an agent reads back and acts on.
2. **Agent identity:** which agent authored a memory or action (non-person-entity identity).
3. **Agent authority:** the set of tool actions an agent may take.

## Adversary
A party who can write to, or tamper with, an agent's memory store or message stream, via indirect prompt injection (the "lethal trifecta": private data + untrusted content + outbound action), a compromised tool/integration, a malicious co-agent, or storage-layer access. Goal: make the agent later act on a falsified "trusted" history, or act with an identity/authority it shouldn't have, **without detection**.

## Attack classes (and SoulGuard's response)
| # | Attack | Example | SoulGuard control | Detected as |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | **Content tampering** | Edit a stored memory after the fact ("no IOC was seen") | Hash-chained entries; stored content must match its hash | `content_tampered` |
| A2 | **Injection / reorder** | Splice a forged memory into history, or reorder entries | Each entry's `prev_hash` must reference the true prior entry | `broken_link` |
| A3 | **Impersonation / persona hijack** | Attribute a memory/action to another agent | Per-agent Ed25519 SoulKey signatures over entry hashes | `bad_signature` |
| A3b | **Signature stripping** | Rebuild the hash chain, then *delete* the signatures rather than forge them | Absence is treated exactly like forgery: on a verified chain, an entry carrying no signature is a finding, not a skipped check | `missing_signature` |
| A4 | **Authority over-reach** | A poisoned agent invokes tools beyond its role | Capability-scoped, short-TTL, signed tokens (least privilege) | token verification fails |
| A5 | **Stale / replayed authority** | Reuse an old capability token | TTL expiry on tokens | token verification fails |

## What SoulGuard does and does not do
**Does:** make A1–A3b *detectable* (silent corruption → raised alarm) and A4–A5 *preventable* (least-privilege, expiring authority); keep the substrate local-first and owned; provide a reproducible ASI06 detection benchmark. Note that A3b is why signature *absence* is a failure rather than a skipped check: an adversary able to rebuild the chain is also able to delete the signatures that would expose the rebuild, so a verifier that only checks signatures it happens to find defends against forgery alone, which is the attack such an adversary has no reason to attempt. Chains predating signing are handled by an explicit, caller-supplied boundary, never by inferring intent from a missing field.
**Does not (v0, residual risk):** prevent the *initial* injection at the input boundary (that's the prompt-firewall layer's job, SoulGuard is the integrity layer beneath it); distinguish *malicious* edits from *authorized* memory evolution at the semantic level (v0 treats the chain as append-only; authorized mutation = a new, signed entry, not an in-place edit); defend a fully-compromised host that holds the signing keys (key custody/HSM is out of scope for v0); detect *tail truncation*, the removal of the newest entries, unless the caller keeps the head hash (`mem.head`) out of band and compares it (added 2026-10-22).

## Trust & key custody assumptions
- The signing secret (governance) and SoulKey private keys are held in the operator's control boundary (local-first). Compromise of the key store is out of scope; SoulGuard is designed so the *memory record itself* is verifiable independent of any single platform.
- Verification is offline-checkable: anyone with the public key + the chain can prove integrity without trusting a service.

## Benchmark protocol (ASI06 v0)
`benchmark/asi06_harness.py` injects A1/A2 attacks into otherwise-clean histories (fixed seed for reproducibility) and reports **detection rate**, **false-positive rate**, and the number of poisoned histories **missed** (corrected 2026-10-22; see the note at the top). The funded roadmap extends this to **adaptive adversaries** and authorized-evolution-vs-tampering precision/recall, the open, measurable benchmark the field currently lacks.

## Roadmap (funded deliverables)
Formal third-party security audit · adaptive-adversary benchmark · MCP-compatible reference adapters · authorized-evolution semantics (distinguishing benign drift from tampering) · key-custody integration (HSM/TPM).

## CONTRIBUTING.md

# Contributing to SoulGuard

SoulGuard is open public-goods AI-security infrastructure. Contributions welcome.

## Principles
- **Sovereignty first.** Anything that makes the user *less* the owner of their agent's memory/identity is out of scope.
- **Verifiable, not trusted.** New controls must be externally checkable (an auditor with the public material can verify them offline).
- **Dependency-light core.** The `memory`, `governance`, and `detection` modules stay standard-library only. Optional crypto/integration deps go in `optional-dependencies`.

## Dev setup
```bash
pip install -e ".[dev]"
python -m pytest            # or: python tests/test_soulguard.py
python examples/quickstart.py
python benchmark/asi06_harness.py
```

## What's most valuable right now
- Adaptive-adversary attacks for the ASI06 benchmark.
- Authorized-evolution-vs-tampering semantics (distinguishing benign memory drift from poisoning).
- MCP-compatible adapters.
- Independent review of the crypto and the threat model (`docs/THREAT_MODEL.md`).
